pages.text: Ancient Greece

image.note: Cover: white temple, blue sea, olive tree

pages.text: Contents. A Land of Small Cities / Athens and the First Democracy / Sparta the Warrior City / The First Olympic Games / Thinkers and Makers / What Greece Gave the World.

Nearly three thousand years ago, on the rocky shores and islands of Greece, a people lived whose ideas still shape your life today. The way you vote. The games you watch. The shape of the word "idea" itself. Much of it began here, among olive trees and white stone.

image.note: Map of ancient Greece, many islands

pages.text: Ancient Greece was not one country. It was a scatter of small cities, each proudly ruling itself, often quarrelling, sometimes at war. Two of them, Athens and Sparta, were so different from each other that together they tell the whole story of Greece.

image.note: Athens and Sparta marked on a map

pages.text: Greece is a land of mountains and sea. Steep ranges cut the land into pockets, and the coast breaks into a thousand islands. It is hard country for one king to rule, and easy country for many small cities to grow, each in its own valley or harbour.

So instead of one great empire, Greece grew as dozens of city-states. Each had its own laws, its own army, its own way of life, and a fierce pride in being different from its neighbours. The Greeks shared a language and gods, but they did not share a ruler.

How small were these cities? Many had fewer people than a single town today. A citizen might know most of his city by sight, and everyone knew everyone's business. A city-state was less like a country and more like one enormous, quarrelsome family.

image.note: Small walled city, everyone knows everyone

pages.text: At the centre of each city stood a high rock called the acropolis, crowned with temples, where people could shelter in danger. Below spread the agora, the open marketplace, where citizens met to trade, argue, gossip, and decide how their city should be run.

It was in these noisy marketplaces, among the fish-sellers and philosophers, that some of the boldest ideas in human history were born. Chief among them was a strange new answer to an old question: who should rule?

Step into the agora on a busy morning. Fish-sellers shout their prices. A potter paints a vase. Two men argue fiercely about a play, while a crowd gathers to listen, for the Greeks would argue about anything, and thought it the finest sport of all.

For most of history, the answer had always been the same. A king should rule, or a handful of powerful families. The city of Athens tried something almost no one had dared before. It let the ordinary people rule themselves. They called it democracy: rule by the people.

Several times a month, the citizens of Athens climbed a hillside to meet in the open air. There, in their thousands, they argued about war, money, and law, and then they voted, each man's hand raised and counted. The decision of the crowd became the law of the city.

image.note: Show of hands on a hillside

pages.text: Imagine you are there. A farmer, sun-browned and plain-spoken, climbs the speaker's stone. He has never met a king, yet here he tells thousands of citizens that they are wrong, and some of them nod. Where else in the ancient world could a farmer do such a thing?

The Athenians even had a way to remove a man who grew too dangerous. Each citizen scratched a name on a piece of broken pot, and if enough names matched, that man was sent away for ten years. From those broken pots, the ostraka, we get our word ostracise: to shut someone out.

image.note: Citizens scratching names on pot shards

pages.text: It was a daring idea, and an unfinished one. Only free men born in Athens could vote. Women could not. Enslaved people could not. Those born elsewhere could not. By our rules today, it was far from fair.

And yet it was a beginning that changed everything. For the first time, a great city was run not by one ruler's word but by the raised hands of its people. Every time you vote for anything, a class captain, a team, a country, you are using an idea first tried on that Athenian hill.

image.note: Modern ballot box beside the ancient hill

pages.text: Athens under this bold experiment blazed with life. It built the most beautiful temple of the ancient world, the Parthenon, high on its acropolis. It filled its theatres with plays still performed today. A city that trusted its people became, for a while, the wonder of Greece.

Building the Parthenon took years and armies of workers: masons, painters, and sculptors, hauling gleaming marble up the steep acropolis. It was painted, once, in bright colours we would hardly recognise today. Time has bleached it white, but in its day it blazed like a jewel above the city.
Now cross the mountains to Athens' great rival, and its opposite in almost every way: Sparta. If Athens lived for ideas, plays, and votes, Sparta lived for one thing only. War.

image.note: Stern Spartan warriors in a line

pages.text: Sparta did not want beautiful temples or clever debates. It wanted the finest army in Greece, and to get it, the whole city was turned into a training camp. Everything, and everyone, served the army.

Spartan children were raised to be tough from the start. Boys left home young for a hard communal school, taught to endure cold, hunger, and pain without complaint, and to become soldiers before they became men. It was a stern and often harsh upbringing.

image.note: Boys at a spare, disciplined school

pages.text: A Spartan boy's day was hard on purpose. He was given too little food, so that he learned to hunt and take what he needed. He was given one thin cloak for the whole year, in summer heat and winter frost alike. Complaining was not allowed. Endurance was everything.

image.note: A lean Spartan boy in a thin cloak

pages.text: There is a famous Spartan saying. When a great enemy sent word, "If we come, we will destroy your city," the Spartans wrote back a single word: "If." They prized few words and cold nerve, and that one word is still remembered thousands of years later.

image.note: A tiny scroll with one word

pages.text: Even Spartan girls trained their bodies and were raised to be strong and fearless, freer in some ways than women elsewhere in Greece, for Sparta wanted strength in everyone.

The result was the most feared army in the Greek world. A small band of Spartans could hold a mountain pass against a mighty foe, and once, famously, a few hundred of them stood against an invading empire to buy their homeland time.

That last stand became one of the most famous in history. A small band held a narrow pass for days against an army so vast that, it was said, their arrows blocked out the sun. "Good," one Spartan is supposed to have replied. "Then we shall fight in the shade."

image.note: Few warriors in a narrow pass, sky dark with arrows

pages.text: Athens and Sparta. One a city of thinkers, one a city of soldiers. In the end they turned on each other in a long and bitter war that exhausted them both. Greece's two greatest cities were, at last, each other's undoing.

image.note: Two cities facing off across a map

pages.text: But the cities of Greece did not only fight. Every four years, they laid down their weapons and came together in peace, for the greatest sporting festival in the world: the Olympic Games.

The Games were held at Olympia, in honour of Zeus, king of the gods. So important were they that a sacred truce was called across all of Greece. Wars were paused. Roads were made safe. For a time, warring cities became rivals only on the running track.

Not everyone could compete. For most of their history the Games were for men only, and married women were not even allowed to watch. But there was a women's festival too, with its own footraces run in honour of a goddess, where girls raced for their own olive crowns.

image.note: Girls racing at their own festival

pages.text: There were foot races, wrestling, boxing, and the throwing of the discus and javelin. Wildest of all were the chariot races, thundering and dangerous, where crashes were common and glory was enormous.

The winners received no money. They received a simple wreath of olive leaves, and something worth far more: undying fame. A victor returned home a hero, honoured for the rest of his life, sometimes with poems and statues in his name.

image.note: Victor crowned with an olive wreath

pages.text: One runner, it was said, was so swift that he was crowned champion of all Greece. His home city was so proud that they did not merely cheer him. They pulled down part of their own city wall, so that such a hero could ride in where no ordinary gate was fit for him.

image.note: Victor riding through a broken wall

pages.text: Those first Games ran for over a thousand years. And though they stopped for a long, long time, the idea never died. The Olympic Games you watch today, with athletes from every nation, are a torch first lit on that field in ancient Greece.

image.note: Ancient torch becoming a modern one

pages.text: The greatest Greek invention of all was not a building or a game. It was a habit of mind: the habit of asking why, and refusing easy answers. The Greeks called a lover of wisdom a philosopher, and they produced the most famous of all time.

One teacher wandered Athens asking simple questions that tied clever people in knots. What is goodness? What is fair? He wrote nothing down, but his way of questioning everything is still taught in schools today. His name was Socrates.

But asking hard questions can make powerful people angry. In the end, the city Socrates loved put him on trial and condemned him, and the old philosopher met his death calmly, still teaching, still refusing to stop asking why. His pupils never forgot him, and neither has the world.

Others measured the world itself. A thinker named Pythagoras found rules hidden in triangles that builders still use. Another worked out that the earth was round, and very nearly measured how big, using only shadows and clever thinking.

Think how astonishing this is. With no rockets and no photographs, using only shadows, sticks, and careful thought, a Greek worked out that the earth was a ball, and very nearly how big around. He was right to within a whisker, more than two thousand years ago.

And there was Archimedes, the cleverest maker of the age. Asked to test a king's crown without breaking it, he puzzled for days, until he stepped into his bath, saw the water rise, and understood. He is said to have leapt out shouting for joy, forgetting to dress, so glad was he to have solved it.

Archimedes built machines that lifted ships and, some say, defended his city with mirrors and cranes. The Greeks showed the world that a single curious mind, armed with nothing but thought, could uncover the hidden rules of everything.

When enemy ships attacked his city, old Archimedes is said to have fought back with machines: great claws of iron that reached down from the walls, caught the ships, and shook them like toys. One clever mind, the story goes, held off a whole fleet.
So what did this land of small quarrelling cities leave behind? More, perhaps, than any empire of its size in history.

From Athens came democracy, the daring idea that people can rule themselves. From Olympia came the Games that still unite the world every four years. From its thinkers came philosophy, mathematics, and science: the habit of asking why.

image.note: Three icons: vote, torch, question mark

pages.text: From its theatres came comedy and tragedy, the very plays and words we still use. Look closely and you will find Greece hidden all through your life: in words like "school", "music", and "idea", each one a gift from that ancient tongue.

Here is a thing to wonder at. When you use the word idea, or theatre, or planet, you are speaking a little Greek. When you vote, or watch the Olympics, or sit in a class at school, you are living out ideas first dreamed on that rocky coast. Greece never really ended. It moved into us.

image.note: Greek words glowing inside modern life

pages.text: Greece was never one great empire. It never needed to be. A handful of small cities, arguing on their rocky coast, thought thoughts so powerful that they outlived every empire around them, and reached all the way to you.

image.note: Greece's ideas radiating across a world map

pages.text: Words to know. City-state: a city that rules itself. Democracy: rule by the people. Citizen: a person with the right to take part. Acropolis: the high fortress of a city. Agora: the marketplace. Philosopher: a lover of wisdom.

Athens and Sparta were only two of hundreds of Greek cities. And Greece was only one land among many great civilisations. Next, we cross the sea to the empire that borrowed from Greece and conquered the world: Rome.
